question: What is the difference between a community and a population?
options: A population includes all species in an area; a community is just one species
A community includes all species in an area; a population is all individuals of one species
A community is the non-living factors in an area; a population is all living things
They mean the same thing
correct: A community includes all species in an area; a population is all individuals of one species

question: Which of the following is an abiotic factor?
options: Predation
Competition
Temperature
Disease

question: What is a producer in a food chain?
options: An animal that eats plants
An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis
A decomposer that breaks down dead material
An animal at the top of the food chain
correct: An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis

question: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
options: Organisms at higher trophic levels are smaller
Energy is lost through heat, movement and waste at each level
Producers absorb all the energy from the sun
Decomposers steal energy from food chains
correct: Energy is lost through heat, movement and waste at each level

question: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
options: To produce food through photosynthesis
To hunt and kill prey
To break down dead organic material and recycle nutrients
To convert nitrogen gas into nitrates
correct: To break down dead organic material and recycle nutrients

question: Which type of bacteria converts nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates?
options: Denitrifying bacteria
Decomposing bacteria
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Nitrifying bacteria

question: What is eutrophication?
options: The build-up of toxic pesticides in organisms at higher trophic levels
The process where excess fertilisers cause algal bloom, reducing oxygen in water
The loss of species due to climate change
The cutting down of forests reducing biodiversity
correct: The process where excess fertilisers cause algal bloom, reducing oxygen in water

question: Which gas is the main driver of the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen

question: What does an indicator species tell us?
options: The total biomass of an ecosystem
The presence or absence of certain environmental conditions
The exact population size of all species in an area
The number of trophic levels in a food web
correct: The presence or absence of certain environmental conditions

question: What is a quadrat used for?
options: To measure the depth of a river
To sample the number and distribution of organisms in an area
To capture and count animals
To test the pH of soil
correct: To sample the number and distribution of organisms in an area

question: Which of the following is a consequence of deforestation?
options: Increased biodiversity due to new habitats
Reduced CO₂ levels in the atmosphere
Loss of habitat and reduced biodiversity
Increased rainfall in the area
correct: Loss of habitat and reduced biodiversity

question: What does a pyramid of biomass show?
options: The number of organisms at each trophic level
The relative biomass at each trophic level
The speed at which energy moves through a food chain
The number of predators and prey in an ecosystem
correct: The relative biomass at each trophic level

question: How does the greenhouse effect cause global warming?
options: Greenhouse gases block sunlight reaching the Earth
Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, trapping heat
Greenhouse gases destroy the ozone layer
Greenhouse gases increase the amount of solar radiation reaching Earth
correct: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, trapping heat

question: What do denitrifying bacteria do?
options: Convert nitrogen gas into nitrates
Break down proteins into ammonia
Convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas
Fix nitrogen into plant roots
correct: Convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas

question: What is interdependence in an ecosystem?
options: When one species drives another to extinction
When organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs
When two species compete for exactly the same resources
When abiotic factors determine which species survive
correct: When organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs

question: All the populations of different species living in the same area is called a __________.
An organism that produces its own food by photosynthesis is called a __________.
Organisms that break down dead material and recycle nutrients are called __________.
The variety of different species in an ecosystem is called __________.
The increase in the Earth's average temperature due to the enhanced greenhouse effect is called __________ warming.
A square frame used to sample organisms in an area is called a __________.
Bacteria that convert nitrogen gas into usable nitrates are called __________ bacteria.
A non-living factor affecting organisms in an ecosystem is called an __________ factor.
The process where excess fertilisers cause algal bloom and oxygen depletion in water is called __________.
The build-up of toxic substances in organisms at higher trophic levels is called __________.
Match each ecological term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: All living organisms and non-living conditions in an area
All the populations of different species in the same area
All individuals of the same species in the same area
The place where an organism lives

question: Match each type of bacteria to its role in the nitrogen cycle.

pairs.definition: Convert nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates
Convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas
Break down dead organic material releasing ammonia

question: Match each human activity to its impact on biodiversity.

pairs.definition: Destroys habitats and reduces species diversity
Excess fertilisers cause algal bloom and kill aquatic life
Pesticides build up in organisms at higher trophic levels
Changes habitats and threatens species unable to adapt

question: Match each feeding term to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Makes its own food by photosynthesis — first in food chain
Eats primary consumers — third trophic level
Breaks down dead organisms returning nutrients to soil

question: Match each sampling method to its use.

pairs.definition: Square frame used to count organisms in a sample area
A line along which organisms are sampled at intervals
Used to estimate population size of mobile animals

question: State the difference between an abiotic and a biotic factor. Give one example of each.
mark_scheme: Abiotic — non-living factor e.g. temperature / light / pH (1); biotic — living factor e.g. predation / competition / disease (1) — accept either for 1 mark.

question: State the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
mark_scheme: Decomposers break down dead organic material (1); releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere through respiration (1) — accept either.

question: Name the sampling method used to investigate how the distribution of organisms changes across an area.
mark_scheme: Transect (1).

question: State what is meant by biodiversity.
mark_scheme: The variety of different species of organisms in an ecosystem or on Earth (1).

question: Explain why energy is lost between trophic levels in a food chain.
mark_scheme: Energy is used for movement / respiration at each trophic level (1); energy is lost as heat (1); some material is not digested and lost as waste (1); only about 10% of energy is passed to the next level (1) — any two.

question: Explain how the greenhouse effect leads to global warming.
mark_scheme: Greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and methane in the atmosphere (1); absorb infrared radiation from the Earth's surface (1); re-emit it back towards Earth (1); trapping heat and raising global temperatures (1) — any two.

question: Describe how eutrophication harms aquatic ecosystems.
mark_scheme: Fertilisers run into water (1); algae grow rapidly forming algal bloom (1); algae block light to plants below (1); plants die (1); decomposers break down dead plants using oxygen (1); oxygen levels fall killing aquatic animals (1) — any two.

question: Explain what is meant by interdependence in an ecosystem.
mark_scheme: Organisms in a community depend on each other (1); for food / shelter / pollination / seed dispersal (1); if one species is removed it can affect others in the community (1) — any two.

question: Explain why sampling is used when studying ecosystems rather than counting every organism.
mark_scheme: Too many organisms to count individually (1); sampling saves time (1); a representative sample can be used to estimate the total population (1); random sampling reduces bias (1) — any two.

question: Explain the role of microorganisms in the nitrogen cycle.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates (1); found in soil or root nodules of leguminous plants (1); decomposers break down proteins in dead organisms releasing ammonia (1); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates (1); denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to nitrogen gas (1) — any three.

question: Describe three ways in which human activities are reducing biodiversity.
mark_scheme: Deforestation destroys habitats (1); eutrophication from fertilisers kills aquatic life (1); global warming changes habitats (1); overhunting / overfishing reduces populations (1); introduction of non-native species outcompetes native species (1); pollution kills organisms (1) — any three.

question: Explain what a pyramid of biomass shows and why it is always pyramid-shaped.
mark_scheme: Shows the relative biomass at each trophic level (1); producers have the most biomass at the base (1); biomass decreases at each higher trophic level (1); because energy and biomass are lost between levels (1); only around 10% of biomass is transferred to the next level (1) — any three.

question: Explain how carbon is cycled through an ecosystem, including the processes of photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.
mark_scheme: Plants absorb CO₂ for photosynthesis (1); carbon incorporated into organic molecules / glucose (1); animals eat plants transferring carbon (1); respiration releases CO₂ back to atmosphere (1); decomposers break down dead organisms releasing CO₂ (1); combustion of fossil fuels releases stored carbon (1) — any four.

question: Explain how a change in one species in a food web can affect other species in the ecosystem.
mark_scheme: Species in a food web are interdependent (1); if a prey species decreases, predator numbers also decrease (1); if a predator is removed, prey numbers increase (1); this may cause another species' food to be depleted (1); changes ripple through the food web (1); ecosystem may become unbalanced (1) — any four.

question: Evaluate the methods used to maintain and increase biodiversity.
mark_scheme: Breeding programmes for endangered species (1); reintroduction to natural habitats (1); protecting habitats / nature reserves (1); reducing deforestation (1); legislation to protect species (1); international agreements on emissions (1); seed banks to preserve plant diversity (1); effectiveness depends on funding and cooperation (1) — any four.

question: Explain how human activities are increasing the rate of global warming and describe the possible consequences.
mark_scheme: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ (1); deforestation reduces CO₂ absorption (1); agriculture produces methane (1); greenhouse gases trap more heat (1); consequences: rising sea levels (1); more extreme weather events (1); loss of habitats and species (1); disruption to food production (1) — any four.

question: Explain the nitrogen cycle, including the roles of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, decomposers, nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen gas makes up 78% of the atmosphere but cannot be used directly (1); nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil or root nodules convert N₂ to ammonia/nitrates (1); plants absorb nitrates and use them to make proteins (1); animals eat plants transferring nitrogen (1); decomposers break down dead organisms releasing ammonia (1); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates (1); denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to N₂ (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the evidence for climate change and the actions that could be taken to reduce its impact. Include both individual and government level actions in your answer.
mark_scheme: Evidence: rising global temperatures recorded over decades (1); melting ice caps and rising sea levels (1); changes in species distribution (1); increased frequency of extreme weather (1). Individual actions: reducing energy use (1); eating less meat (1); using public transport (1). Government actions: international agreements e.g. Paris Agreement (1); investment in renewable energy (1); regulation of emissions (1); protecting forests (1) — any six.

question: Explain why maintaining biodiversity is important and describe the human activities that threaten it and the conservation methods that can protect it.
mark_scheme: Biodiversity provides ecosystem stability (1); provides food, medicine and materials (1); loss of one species can have knock-on effects (1). Threats: deforestation (1); pollution / eutrophication (1); climate change (1); overhunting (1). Conservation: nature reserves (1); breeding programmes (1); reintroduction of species (1); international agreements (1); reducing pollution (1) — any six.

question: Explain what is meant by a 'community' and an 'ecosystem'. Include the difference between biotic and abiotic factors.
mark_scheme: Community: all the organisms (populations of different species) living in an area (1); ecosystem: a community of organisms and the non-living environment they interact with (1); biotic factors: living factors affecting organisms, e.g. competition, predation (1); abiotic factors: non-living factors, e.g. temperature, light intensity, pH (1).

question: Describe what happens to energy as it passes along a food chain. Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
mark_scheme: Energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (1); only about 10% of energy is transferred — most lost as heat (respiration), some in faeces/urine (1); less energy available at each level — so fewer organisms can be supported (1); beyond 4–5 levels, too little energy remains to support a viable population (1).

question: Explain the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle. Include what decomposers are and how they release carbon back into the atmosphere.
mark_scheme: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi (1); they break down dead organic matter — detritivores also help by mechanical breakdown (1); decomposers respire aerobically — release CO₂ into atmosphere (1); this returns carbon from living matter back to the atmosphere — completing the carbon cycle (1).

question: Describe the conditions that affect the rate of decomposition. Include temperature, moisture and oxygen availability.
mark_scheme: Temperature: higher temperature increases enzyme activity in decomposers — faster decomposition (up to optimum) (1); moisture: water needed for decomposer activity — too dry slows decomposition (1); oxygen: aerobic decomposers need O₂ — waterlogged or compacted soils slow decomposition (1); pH: neutral to slightly acidic is optimal — very acidic soils (e.g. peat bogs) preserve organic matter (1).

question: Explain why maintaining high biodiversity is important for ecosystems and for humans.
mark_scheme: High biodiversity: more stable ecosystems — greater resilience to change (1); provides many ecosystem services: pollination, water purification, soil formation (1); source of medicines and food crops — many drugs derived from plants (1); loss of one species can affect whole food web — reduces ecosystem stability (1).

question: Describe how human activities are causing climate change. Include two specific human activities and the gases involved.
mark_scheme: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ (1); deforestation removes trees that absorb CO₂ — also releases CO₂ (1); rice paddies and livestock farming produce methane (CH₄) (1); these greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere — leading to rising global temperatures (1).

question: Explain how organisms compete for resources in an ecosystem. Include examples of interspecific and intraspecific competition.
mark_scheme: Intraspecific competition: between individuals of the same species for same resources (1); e.g. robins competing for territory and food (1); interspecific competition: between different species for similar resources (1); e.g. red squirrels and grey squirrels competing for nuts and habitat — grey squirrel outcompetes red (1).

question: Describe the main stages of the nitrogen cycle. Include the roles of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil/root nodules convert N₂ gas to ammonium compounds (1); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium → nitrites → nitrates (1); plants absorb nitrates through roots — use them to make proteins (1); denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to N₂ gas — complete the cycle (1).

question: Evaluate the effectiveness of conservation programmes in maintaining biodiversity. Include captive breeding and habitat protection as examples.
mark_scheme: Captive breeding: prevents extinction; individuals reintroduced to wild — e.g. Arabian oryx (1); but: small gene pool → inbreeding; animals may struggle to survive in wild (1); habitat protection: preserves entire ecosystem including all species (1); but: requires large areas; difficult to enforce against economic pressures (1).

question: Explain how predator and prey populations are linked. Describe what happens to prey numbers if the predator population increases.
mark_scheme: Predator and prey populations fluctuate in cycles (1); predator numbers follow prey with a time delay (1); if predators increase: more prey eaten — prey population falls (1); fewer prey → less food for predators → predator numbers fall → prey population recovers (1).

question: Describe two ways in which climate change could affect ecosystems and species distributions.
mark_scheme: Rising temperatures: species shift their range towards poles or higher altitudes to remain in suitable conditions (1); e.g. UK butterflies moving north (1); disruption of breeding seasons: animals breed earlier — may not align with food availability (1); coral bleaching: warmer seas cause corals to expel algae — reefs die — loss of habitat for hundreds of species (1).

question: Explain the concept of trophic levels and explain how the shape of an energy pyramid reflects the efficiency of energy transfer.
mark_scheme: Trophic level 1: producers (plants) — trap energy from sunlight by photosynthesis (1); trophic level 2: primary consumers (herbivores) — eat plants (1); each trophic level receives ~10% of energy from level below (1); pyramid shape: wide base (producers) → narrower at top — less energy available at each level (1); explains why top predators are rare and why there are few trophic levels (1).

question: Describe the carbon cycle. Include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion and the ocean as a carbon store.
mark_scheme: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from atmosphere — stored as glucose in plants (1); respiration by all organisms releases CO₂ (1); decomposers break down dead matter — release CO₂ through respiration (1); combustion of fossil fuels and wood releases stored carbon as CO₂ (1); oceans absorb CO₂ — stored in water as carbonate ions; marine organisms form carbonate shells (1).

question: Evaluate the measures that can be taken to reduce the impact of climate change. Include both personal and national/global level actions.
mark_scheme: Personal: reduce energy use, eat less meat, use public transport — reduces individual carbon footprint (1); national: renewable energy targets — wind, solar replace fossil fuels (1); reforestation: planting trees absorbs CO₂ — carbon sequestration (1); global: international agreements (Paris Agreement) set targets to limit warming (1); limitation: economic development in poorer nations requires energy; political disagreement slows action (1).

question: Explain how human activities reduce biodiversity. Include deforestation, pollution, and introduction of invasive species as examples.
mark_scheme: Deforestation: removes habitat, destroys ecosystems, many species lost (1); causes soil erosion and reduces water retention (1); pollution: pesticides/herbicides kill non-target species (1); introduction of invasive species: outcompete native species — reduce diversity e.g. grey squirrel vs red squirrel (1); climate change: alters habitats faster than species can adapt — causes extinctions (1).

question: Describe how to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decomposition in a controlled experiment. Include the variables and how to measure decomposition.
mark_scheme: Set up identical containers of leaf litter or compost (1); place at different temperatures (e.g. 5°C, 15°C, 25°C, 35°C) (1); measure mass loss over time — as organic matter decomposes, mass decreases (1); control variables: amount of material, moisture level, oxygen availability, type of material (1); repeat at each temperature and average to reduce error (1).

question: Explain the effects on a food web of removing a species from the middle of the chain (a 'keystone species'). Use a named example to support your answer.
mark_scheme: A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance (1); e.g. sea otters eat sea urchins — urchins eat kelp (1); without otters, sea urchins increase — kelp forests destroyed (1); many species depend on kelp for habitat and food — cascade effect through food web (1); removing middle species can cause both prey to increase and predators to decline — 'trophic cascade' (1).

question: Evaluate the importance of international cooperation in protecting global biodiversity. Include specific threats and examples of conservation efforts.
mark_scheme: Many species and habitats cross national boundaries — single country cannot protect them alone (1); deforestation in Amazon affects global climate — needs international action (1); Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) — restricts trade in threatened species (1); global seed banks (Svalbard) preserve crop genetic diversity (1); challenges: developing nations prioritise economic growth over conservation; enforcement difficult (1).

question: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect and describe the evidence that climate change is caused by human activity.
mark_scheme: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) trap infrared radiation — warm Earth's surface (1); enhanced greenhouse effect: increased concentrations due to human activity amplify warming (1); ice core evidence: CO₂ concentration closely tracks temperature over 800,000 years (1); CO₂ concentration increased from ~280 ppm pre-industrial to >420 ppm now — correlates with industrialisation (1); carbon isotope ratios in CO₂ show the carbon is from fossil fuels (1).

question: Describe the water cycle and explain how changes in vegetation cover can affect it.
mark_scheme: Evaporation from oceans/lakes — water vapour rises (1); condensation: water vapour cools and forms clouds (1); precipitation: rain or snow falls on land (1); transpiration from plants adds water vapour — significant especially in forests (1); deforestation reduces transpiration — less rainfall in deforested areas; increased surface runoff — flooding (1).

question: Evaluate the use of indicator species to monitor environmental pollution. Include examples of both water and air pollution indicators.
mark_scheme: Water pollution: mayfly larvae only present in clean water — absence indicates pollution (1); bloodworms tolerate low O₂ — presence suggests organic pollution (1); air pollution: lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide — lichen diversity indicates air quality (1); advantages: cheap, continuous monitoring, reflect real biological impact (1); limitations: species distribution affected by factors other than pollution; cannot identify specific pollutants (1).

question: Explain the nitrogen cycle in detail. Include all processes and the organisms involved at each stage.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen gas (N₂) makes up 78% of atmosphere but most organisms cannot use it directly (1); nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules fix N₂ to ammonium (NH₄⁺) (1); nitrification: Nitrosomonas converts ammonium to nitrite; Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate — aerobic process (1); plants absorb nitrates — used to make amino acids and proteins (1); animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants/other animals; excretion returns nitrogen to soil as urea/ammonia (1); denitrification: anaerobic bacteria convert nitrates back to N₂ — in waterlogged soils (1).

question: Evaluate the consequences of climate change for ecosystems and biodiversity. Include both direct and indirect effects and consider different geographical regions.
mark_scheme: Rising temperatures: species shift range poleward or to higher altitude — some cannot migrate fast enough (1); coral bleaching: ocean warming above 1°C above normal causes mass bleaching events — threatens 25% of marine species (1); polar regions: Arctic ice loss — polar bears, seals, penguins lose habitat (1); tropical regions: increased drought frequency and intensity — savanna turning to desert (1); indirect effects: food web disruption — seasonal timing mismatch between predators and prey (1); some species may benefit — invasive species expand range; overall biodiversity loss is the dominant trend (1).

question: Describe the main threats to biodiversity and evaluate the effectiveness of international and local conservation strategies to address them.
mark_scheme: Threats: habitat destruction (agriculture, urbanisation, deforestation) is the primary cause of species loss (1); overexploitation — hunting, overfishing — reduces populations below viable levels (1); pollution destroys freshwater and marine habitats (1); invasive species outcompete natives (1); international: CITES limits trade in endangered species; Ramsar Convention protects wetlands (1); local: nature reserves, corridor habitats, rewilding — reintroducing lost species like beavers in UK (1). Accept: limited effectiveness without funding/enforcement; biodiversity still declining globally.

question: Explain how energy flows through an ecosystem. Include the original source of energy, the role of producers and consumers, and why energy is lost at each trophic level.
mark_scheme: Solar energy is absorbed by producers (plants) during photosynthesis — converted to chemical energy in glucose (1); only ~1% of solar energy actually fixed (1); producers eaten by primary consumers — energy transferred (1); only ~10% of energy transferred at each trophic level (1); energy lost as: heat through respiration, energy in faeces/urine not absorbed by consumer (1); this explains pyramids of biomass and number — why top predators are rare and require large territory (1).

question: Evaluate the role of zoos and captive breeding programmes in conserving endangered species. Include successes, limitations and the ethics of keeping wild animals in captivity.
mark_scheme: Successes: Arabian oryx, California condor, black-footed ferret — brought back from brink of extinction (1); captive breeding creates insurance populations (1); zoos educate public — increase conservation awareness and funding (1); limitations: small captive populations have limited genetic diversity — inbreeding depression (1); reintroduction success rate low — animals may lack survival skills or suitable habitat no longer exists (1); ethics: wild animals in captivity may have reduced welfare; zoo resources could fund in-situ conservation instead (1).

question: Explain how increased levels of CO₂ and methane in the atmosphere lead to global warming. Include the origin of each gas and the mechanism by which they trap heat.
mark_scheme: CO₂ released by burning fossil fuels — concentrations rising since industrial revolution (1); methane produced by livestock, rice paddies, landfill sites (1); both are greenhouse gases — their molecules absorb and re-emit infrared radiation (1); Earth's surface absorbs solar radiation and emits infrared (heat) (1); greenhouse gases trap this heat in the lower atmosphere — raising surface temperature (1); feedback loops: warming melts Arctic permafrost releasing stored methane — amplifies warming further (1).

question: Evaluate the ecological and economic arguments for and against rewilding large areas of land. Include specific examples and consider the perspective of local communities.
mark_scheme: Rewilding: reintroducing lost species and allowing natural processes to take over (1); ecological benefits: reintroduction of wolves in Yellowstone changed river courses (trophic cascade) — transformed ecosystem (1); beavers reintroduced in UK — reduce flooding, improve water quality (1); economic benefits: ecotourism — wildlife watching generates local income (1); economic concerns: farmers lose land; wolves/lynx may prey on livestock (1); local community perspective: must involve communities and provide compensation schemes for success (1).

question: Describe the role of decomposers and detritivores in nutrient cycling. Explain why decomposition is essential for the continuation of life on Earth.
mark_scheme: Detritivores (earthworms, woodlice) mechanically break down dead material into smaller pieces — increasing surface area (1); bacteria and fungi (decomposers) secrete enzymes that chemically break down organic molecules (1); decomposers respire — releasing CO₂ (carbon cycle) (1); nitrogen in proteins released as ammonium compounds — nitrifying bacteria convert to nitrates (1); without decomposers: dead material would accumulate, nutrients locked up — plants could not grow (1); decomposition essential for nutrient cycling — same atoms used repeatedly; life depends on this recycling (1).

question: Explain how the removal of a top predator from a food web can have cascading effects throughout the ecosystem. Use specific examples to illustrate your answer.
mark_scheme: Top predators regulate prey populations — their removal causes prey to increase unchecked (1); e.g. removal of sharks: fish populations surge, overgrazing of seagrass (1); increased herbivores overgraze vegetation — habitat degraded (1); other species dependent on that vegetation decline (1); shows interdependence in ecosystems — changing one species affects all (1).

question: Give one example of a biotic factor and one example of an abiotic factor that affect organisms in an ecosystem.
mark_scheme: Biotic: any living factor e.g. predation / competition / disease (1); abiotic: any non-living factor e.g. temperature / light intensity / pH / water availability (1).

question: Explain why there is less energy available at each successive trophic level in a food chain.
mark_scheme: Energy is lost at each level through respiration as heat (1); and through waste products such as faeces that are not passed to the next level (1).

question: State the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the atmosphere (1); into ammonia or nitrates that plants can absorb and use (1).

question: Explain how deforestation reduces biodiversity.
mark_scheme: Deforestation destroys the habitat of many species (1); organisms that depend on the forest for food and shelter lose their habitat and may become extinct (1).

question: Give two human activities that are increasing carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere.
mark_scheme: Any two from: burning fossil fuels (1); deforestation — trees absorb less CO₂ (1); burning wood or biomass (1).

question: State why random sampling is important when using quadrats to estimate population size.
mark_scheme: Random sampling avoids bias (1); it ensures the sample is representative of the whole area (1).

question: Explain the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
mark_scheme: Decomposers break down dead organic matter (1); they release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere through respiration (1).

question: Give two examples of how organisms in an ecosystem depend on each other.
mark_scheme: Any two from: predator depends on prey for food (1); plants depend on insects for pollination (1); organisms depend on decomposers to recycle nutrients (1); prey depends on producers for energy (1).

question: State what is meant by a species being an indicator species. Give one example.
mark_scheme: An indicator species is an organism whose presence or absence indicates the quality of environmental conditions (1); e.g. mayfly larvae indicate clean water / lichens indicate clean air (1).

question: Compare the use of quadrats and transects for sampling organisms.
mark_scheme: Quadrats are used to measure the abundance or percentage cover of organisms in a sample area (1); transects are used to show how the distribution of organisms changes across an area or gradient (1).

question: Explain the role of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle, naming three different types and their functions.
mark_scheme: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ gas into ammonia or nitrates for plants (1); nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrates in the soil (1); denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas (1).

question: Describe three human activities that are causing a reduction in biodiversity.
mark_scheme: Any three from: deforestation removes habitat (1); eutrophication from fertiliser run-off kills aquatic life (1); climate change alters habitats faster than species can adapt (1); overhunting reduces population sizes (1); introduction of non-native invasive species outcompetes native species (1).

question: Explain what a pyramid of biomass shows and why it is always pyramid-shaped.
mark_scheme: A pyramid of biomass shows the relative mass of organisms at each trophic level (1); producers have the greatest biomass at the base (1); biomass decreases at each higher trophic level because energy is lost between levels (1); only about 10% of biomass is transferred from one level to the next (1) — any three.

question: Describe how predator and prey populations are linked, and what happens to prey numbers when predator numbers increase.
mark_scheme: Predator and prey populations are interdependent and fluctuate in cycles (1); if predator numbers increase, more prey are eaten so prey population decreases (1); fewer prey means less food for predators so predator numbers then fall (1); prey population recovers as predation pressure decreases (1) — any three.

question: Explain how the enhanced greenhouse effect leads to global warming.
mark_scheme: Human activities release greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and methane into the atmosphere (1); these gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface (1); they re-emit it back towards Earth, trapping heat (1); the increased concentration of greenhouse gases means more heat is trapped, raising global temperatures (1) — any three.

question: Describe how the capture-recapture method is used to estimate the size of an animal population.
mark_scheme: A sample of animals is captured, marked and released back into the population (1); after time a second sample is captured (1); the number of marked individuals in the second sample is recorded (1); population size is estimated using: (first capture × second capture) ÷ number recaptured marked (1) — any three.

question: Explain how the carbon cycle maintains a balance of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
mark_scheme: Plants absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis, storing carbon in organic molecules (1); organisms release CO₂ back to the atmosphere through respiration (1); decomposers release CO₂ when they break down dead organic matter (1); combustion of fossil fuels also releases stored carbon as CO₂ — human activities are disrupting this balance (1) — any three.

question: Describe how eutrophication leads to the death of aquatic organisms.
mark_scheme: Excess fertilisers run off into water (1); algae grow rapidly forming an algal bloom which blocks light to aquatic plants (1); plants die and decomposers multiply, using up dissolved oxygen (1); aquatic animals die due to lack of oxygen (1) — any three.

question: Explain the difference between interspecific and intraspecific competition. Give an example of each.
mark_scheme: Intraspecific competition occurs between individuals of the same species competing for the same resources (1); e.g. robins competing with other robins for territory (1); interspecific competition occurs between different species competing for similar resources (1); e.g. grey squirrels and red squirrels competing for food and habitat (1) — any three.

question: Describe two consequences of global warming for living organisms.
mark_scheme: Rising temperatures cause species to shift their range towards the poles or higher altitudes to remain in suitable conditions (1); disruption of breeding seasons — animals may breed earlier, which may not align with food availability (1); coral bleaching — warmer oceans cause corals to expel algae, damaging reef ecosystems (1); some species unable to adapt fast enough may become extinct (1) — any three.

question: Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
mark_scheme: Energy is lost at each trophic level through respiration and waste (1); only about 10% of energy is transferred from one level to the next (1); by the time you reach the fourth or fifth trophic level, so little energy remains that it cannot support a viable population (1).

question: Describe three methods used to protect and conserve endangered species.
mark_scheme: Any three from: captive breeding programmes to increase population size and reintroduce to the wild (1); habitat protection / nature reserves to preserve ecosystems (1); seed banks to preserve genetic material of plant species (1); legal protection / legislation to prevent hunting or habitat destruction (1); international agreements such as CITES to limit trade in endangered species (1).
